newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banks reject Holocaust boycott threat.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks reject Holocaust boycott threat.

text.p: Swiss banks on Monday rejected threats of a boycott from world Jewish groups, saying any such action would not help joint efforts to find the lost bank accounts of Holocaust victims.

The Swiss Bankers Association said it hoped Jewish groups would remain a constructive partner in a joint commission set up last May to oversee the hunt for dormant accounts left by Jews killed by the Nazis.
"The Swiss Bankers Association does not regard sanction and boycott threats or ultimatums as an appropriate means to foster the work already started," the umbrella organisation said in a statement.
It also noted that an agreement creating the commission, headed by former U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Paul Volcker, was signed by some of the same Jewish representatives now threatening a boycott.
"The Swiss Bankers Association hopes that the Jewish organisations will maintain a constructive attitude towards the jointly initiated efforts at clarification," it said.
Separately, the bank association's president Georg Krayer said a withdrawal of international business could have a considerable effect on Swiss banks.

Switzerland's three biggest banks -- Union Bank of Switzerland, Credit Suisse Group and Swiss Bank Corp -- would be most vulnerable because of their world role in asset management for investment and pension funds.
Krayer said the size of losses from a Jewish boycott was "difficult to estimate today" but could be "considerable", according to excerpts of a Swiss radio interview.
Swiss bank shares lost ground in selling that traders blamed in part on the renewed talk of a world Jewish boycott.
Bearer shares in Union Bank of Switzerland, the country's biggest bank, fell 21 Swiss francs or 1.8 percent to close at 1,149 francs.
Credit Suisse Group was down 2.0 percent or 2.75 francs at 133.75. Swiss Bank Corp lost 0.6 percent or 1.50 francs to 252.50 Swiss francs.

Traders said institutional investors sold Swiss bank shares following headlines over the latest twist in a long-standing dispute with Jewish groups over how much money might be in dormant Swiss accounts left by Jews murdered in the Holocaust.
"This is one reason for investment funds taking their leave from bank shares," one Zurich trader told Reuters.

Boycott worries were raised by news reports the World Jewish Congress (WJC) and the quasi governmental Jewish Agency, which helps Jews immigrate to Israel, were considering a call for Jews to shun Swiss banks.

Boycott proposals have been raised several times in recent months as a way to force Swiss banks to speed up the hunt for Holocaust accounts or to force the Swiss government to set up a compensation fund for heirs of Holocaust victims.
The WJC said on December 13 it had postponed until late January a decision on whether to urge Jewish money be taken out of Swiss banks.

This time, WJC vice-president Israel Singer and Jewish Agency chairman Avraham Burg were reported to have told a news conference they were considering a boycott in response to claims by outgoing Swiss president Jean-Pascal Delamuraz that calls for a compensation fund were "blackmail".

Burg is one of three Jewish-appointed members of the seven-person Volcker commission, whose job is to make sure Swiss banks do a thorough job of hunting for Holocuast accounts and finding any heirs to the owners.

The commission is separate from an international historical panel set up in December by Berne to report on the extent and fate of Jewish wealth and Nazi loot sent to neutral Switzerland during the war.
